question: At the year end Kestrel owes its staff an £8m bonus that it will pay in March. Tax is 25 %. Walk me through this year's statements, then what happens in March.
model_answer_md:
**This year — the accrual.**

- **Income statement.** The bonus was earned this year, so it is an expense now even though no cash has moved: operating costs +£8m, tax −£2m, **net income −£6m**.
- **Cash flow statement.** Start at −£6m. The **increase in accrued liabilities** (bills owed but not yet paid) is added back, **+£8m**. Cash **rises £2m**, which is the tax saving.
- **Balance sheet.** Cash +2. Accrued liabilities +8. Retained earnings −6. Assets +2 = liabilities +8 + equity −6, so it balances.

**In March — the payment.** No income statement effect, because the expense has already been booked. Operating cash flow shows the **decrease in accrued liabilities, −£8m**. Cash −8 and accrued liabilities −8.
key_points: Expense is recognised when earned, not when paid
This year: NI −6, cash +2, accrued liabilities +8
The accrual is added back as a working-capital movement
Payment next year: cash −8, accrued −8, no income statement effect

follow_ups.question: Why does cash rise this year if the company has a new cost?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because nothing has been paid yet, but the expense still reduces taxable profit. The only cash effect this year is £2m less tax. The £8m leaves in March.

follow_ups.question: How is a prepayment the mirror image?
follow_ups.answer_md: A prepayment is cash paid before the expense is recognised. Cash leaves first and the asset unwinds into expense later. An accrual is expense recognised first and cash paid later.

weak_answer_note: Says no expense until the bonus is paid (cash accounting), or forgets the tax effect and says cash is unchanged this year.
